newsitem.title: UK: Timetable for opening UK gas market still uncertain.
newsitem.headline: Timetable for opening UK gas market still uncertain.

text.p: The timetable for opening the whole of the UK's domestic natural gas market to competition remains uncertain, although a spokesman for pipeline operator Transco said on Friday that a starting date of next April was their preferred option.

Transco, part of BG Plc, says it is committed to "the earliest practicable implementation of domestic competition," and the spokesman added that the interpretation of the word "practicable" is at the heart of any discussion over when it starts.

In particular, installing the necessary Information Technology systems and testing them fully must be completed before any start date can be considered practicable, and there are persistent doubts over whether this can be achieved.

Industry regulator Ofgas will not comment on its favoured start up date. A spokeswoman said on Friday that "Ofgas is publishing a consultation document early next week. This will set out its views in detail on extending competition further," but would not add any details.
But Ofgas has in the past made clear its view that competition should start as soon as possible.

Under the Gas Act of 1995, opening the market to competition was scheduled to start in 1998, after trials starting in 1996 in Devon, Somerset and Cornwall, and in 1997 in Avon, Dorset, East and West Sussex and Kent.
The trials have gone ahead as planned, but Ian Lang, then President of the Board of Trade, announced a new timetable for full opening in March.
He then proposed a timetable starting in October 1997 in Scotland and North East England and finishing in April 1998, with new areas brought in every month between these dates.

Transco says that the industry has already achieved a lot from the pilot areas, and a spokesman added that the company "will continue doing its utmost to achieve its part of the industry's plan, working constructively with other participants."

But he also added "April would be good for us," saying Transco had always envisaged a programme starting next April and finishing towards the end of the year until Ian Lang made his surprise announcement.
Energy Minister John Battle has said he will not be tied to the timetable set by the outgoing government.
"We're not interested in slowing down competition but...what's starting to worry us is that the lessons of the southwest have not yet been learnt in terms of consumers' rights," he said last month.
